newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Archives cast dark light on Swiss WWII role.
newsitem.headline: Archives cast dark light on Swiss WWII role.

text.p: Swiss diplomatic archives published for the first time on Wednesday showed Nazi Germany got the bulk of Swiss arms exports during World War Two and that the Swiss central bank may have known it was buying looted Nazi gold.

Historians said the disclosures were nothing new, but they nevertheless kept a harsh spotlight on neutral Switzerland's controversial role as a wartime financial centre with close commercial ties to Hitler's Germany.

Swiss historian Mauro Cerutti, a researcher who studied the archives, said Nazi Germany got nearly two-thirds of Swiss exports of arms and war material from 1940 to 1944. It received arms worth 600 million Swiss francs at the time.
Fascist Italy got another 150 million francs worth of arms out of total wartime exports of 900 million. The dollar was worth around four Swiss francs at the war's end.
"These are official figures. They are very precise," Cerutti told reporters. "Arms exports ended only at the end of September 1944 following pressure from the Allies."
Other historians said publication of the documents, which had only been open to scholars in the past, supported previous studies of Swiss arms sales to Nazi Germany.
"This is not new, but it still interesting because all these bits of information had been stranded among historic researchers," said Peter Hug, who has studied the wartime era.

Another document suggested the Swiss National Bank (SNB) may have known it was buying gold that Germany plundered from the countries it occupied, despite the central bank's assertions that it had been misled by German bankers it trusted.

A letter dated June 19, 1946 from then-SNB head Paul Rossy to the finance minister declared that another bank director, Alfred Hirs, had "in 1943 and 1944 bought from Reichsbank looted Belgian gold knowing the origin and the nature of this gold.
"I believe that the Federal Council (cabinet) cannot tolerate that Hirs stays in the general management after such behaviour," according to the letter.

The documents came hot on the heels of a scathing U.S. government report published earlier this month, rejected in part by Berne, which alleged the Swiss were bankers to the Nazis and their trade with Nazi Germany helped to prolong World War Two.

Swiss officials have said Switzerland had to trade with Nazi Germany and Berlin's fascist partners surrounding the Alpine republic because it needed food and fuel to survive. Switzerland also traded with the Allies, and provided arms to them as well.

Cerutti said the documents revealed much about Switzerland's wartime record, which the country has been desperately trying to defend with its moral integrity intact against mounting international criticism that it cynically profited from the war.
But he said they were limited to federal government files and that questions still remained about the archives in the vaults of Swiss banks, among the world's most secretive.
In Berne, the government elected one of Switzerland's most vocal critics, World Jewish Congress (WJC) President Edgar Bronfman, as a member of the panel running a memorial fund for Holocaust victims.

Bronfman replaced Nobel Prize-inning author Elie Wiesel, who was nominated to the seven-member board but declined to take up the post of chairman for the 265 million Swiss franc ($186.4 million) fund financed by Swiss banks and private businesses.
Bronfman has led the WJC's fight over unclaimed Jewish assets in Switzerland. Jewish groups accuse Swiss banks of hoarding dormant wealth of Holocaust victims, which banks deny.

Wiesel bowed out from the fund's board, citing negative comments in the Swiss press and after Swiss officials made clear his title of international chairman carried no special powers. WJC officials said this had insulted Wiesel.

Four of the fund's members are named by the Swiss government and three by the World Jewish Restitution Organisation, a branch of the WJC. WJC Executive Director Elan Steinberg has said Bronfman will serve only until a permanent replacement is found.

A government statement said the cabinet had also elected 18 representatives to the fund's advisory board, which will propose how to distribute funds to needy recipients who were persecuted by the Nazis because of their race, religion or politics.
It includes representatives of gypsies, the handicapped, charities and homosexuals as well as of Jewish groups and Holocaust survivors.
"The Federal Council now hopes that the Special Fund in support of needy Holocaust victims, who are elderly, can soon take up its work," the statement said.
